turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through the project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.adopted: none
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, first suspicion, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a wrong price that only showed up sometimes. It happened when a user tapped options quickly, one after another. I first suspected the price index itself, that it was built wrong. But the logs showed the index was correct every time. The real cause was an old calculation finishing late and overwriting the newer result. A repro with fast taps on one device showed it every time, and that proved my first guess wrong.
card.then: Next: how I fixed it and how I checked the fix.

more: The fix was to tag each calculation with a request ID and ignore any result whose ID was out of date. I also cancel the old job when a new tap comes in. To check it, I tapped options fast on a slow test device and watched the logs. The price always matched the last tap. One trade-off is that cancelling the old job can leave a brief window where no result is shown, so I keep the last confirmed price visible until the new one arrives.

turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Walk through the project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.adopted: none
card.heard: other options, why not, and how I knew it worked after release
card.say: I had two other options. One was to lock the calculation with a mutex, so only one ran at a time. The other was to keep a single latest-result field and only accept a result that matched the current selection. I didn't pick the mutex because it makes every tap wait for the one before it, so fast taps feel slow. The single field is close to what I did, but a request ID is clearer in the logs, so I can see which result was dropped. After release, I checked two things. The crash-free rate stayed the same, and no new price complaints came in. I also kept the fast-tap test as a regression test, so the same bug can't come back quietly.
card.then: Next, I can say what I'd do differently if the price came from the server instead of the phone.

more: The first thing was the crash-free rate and the ANR rate in our release dashboard. They stayed normal, so the change didn't break anything. The second thing was the price itself. I went through the booking flow myself on a slow phone and tapped options fast. The price always matched the last tap. I didn't have a formal user feedback channel for this page, so I checked it myself and watched the logs for dropped results.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the repository saves the intent with its client ID in the local database before calling the API — what exactly gets written in that row, and how does the app use it if the process dies mid-request?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Client, server and local storage: server owns the ledger, phone caches reads and saves the transfer intent before sending
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer history and details are in scope; cached reads work offline", "Submitting money needs the network; the server owns the authoritative ledger", "Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope", "A has 100 dollars and B has 0"]
card.heard: what gets written, and process death mid-request
card.say: The row holds the client transfer ID, the payer, the payee, the amount as 8000 cents, and a status of pending. It's written to the local database before the API call, so it survives process death. After a restart, the app reads that pending row and asks the server for the status by account and client ID. It only resends the same ID, and only as the server's idempotency contract allows. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
card.then: Next, what the result screen shows while the outcome is still unknown.

more: It also carries a timestamp and an attempt count, so a retry has a limit. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight. The result screen shows four states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown. It only shows success from the server's transfer record.

Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The problem was that planning a trip by hand takes a lot of time.
Candidate: You work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together yourself.
Candidate: Our planner took a destination, a budget and a number of days, and gave back a trip the user could book.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan: the agent design, the product and order tools, and the core backend.
Candidate: It ended at the Android side of the result display, which I wrote with the app team.
Candidate: On the user side, it was travelers on our Android app in many markets.
Candidate: They wanted a trip they could book, not just a list of ideas.
Candidate: My responsibility ended where the app team's own screens began.
Candidate: I agreed the card format with them, but they built those screens.
Candidate: The part I owned was the agent, the tools, the backend, and the Android code that reads the streamed plan.

Interviewer: You said your responsibility ended where the app team's screens began, yet you also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan. In that trip planner, which exact pieces did you build yourself versus the team?
Candidate: I built the agent design, the product and order tools, and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream of the plan.
Candidate: The app team built the screens around it, and I agreed the card format with them.
Candidate: The personalization data layer was mine too.
Candidate: The personalization data layer was mine too.
Candidate: It uses search history, preferences and past purchases.
Candidate: Both trip planning and search recommendations sit on it.
Candidate: The app team built the screens around the cards.
Candidate: I agreed the card format with them.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: I'll take the SKU page at KKday, because I changed that logic myself.
Candidate: A user taps a ticket type.
Candidate: Before, every tap recalculated all the price and stock combinations on the main thread.
Candidate: I flattened the configuration and built a price and stock index ahead of time.
Candidate: Then I moved the calculation to Dispatchers.Default and sent results out through StateFlow.
Candidate: One edge case: if the user taps again before the first result returns, I cancel the previous job so a stale price can't overwrite the newer selection.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a wrong price that only showed up sometimes.
Candidate: It happened when a user tapped options quickly, one after another.
Candidate: I first suspected the price index itself, that it was built wrong.
Candidate: But the logs showed the index was correct every time.
Candidate: The real cause was an old calculation finishing late and overwriting the newer result.
Candidate: A repro with fast taps on one device showed it every time, and that proved my first guess wrong.
Candidate: The fix was to tag each calculation with a request ID and ignore any result whose ID was out of date.
Candidate: I also cancel the old job when a new tap comes in.
Candidate: To check it, I tapped options fast on a slow test device and watched the logs.
Candidate: The price always matched the last tap.
Candidate: One trade-off is that cancelling the old job can leave a brief window where no result is shown, so I keep the last confirmed price visible until the new one arrives.
Interviewer: You said a repro with fast taps on one device showed it every time — how did you confirm that stale-result race was the actual cause and not just correlated with fast tapping?
Candidate: I made the race happen on purpose.
Candidate: I added a short delay to the old calculation, so it always finished after the new one.
Candidate: The wrong price came back every time.
Candidate: With the delay removed, it stopped.
Candidate: That showed the late result was the cause, not just fast tapping.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had two other options.
Candidate: One was to lock the calculation with a mutex, so only one ran at a time.
Candidate: The other was to keep a single latest-result field and only accept a result that matched the current selection.
Candidate: I didn't pick the mutex because it makes every tap wait for the one before it, so fast taps feel slow.
Candidate: The single field is close to what I did, but a request ID is clearer in the logs, so I can see which result was dropped.
Candidate: After release, I checked two things.
Candidate: The crash-free rate stayed the same, and no new price complaints came in.
Candidate: I also kept the fast-tap test as a regression test, so the same bug can't come back quietly.
Candidate: The first thing was the crash-free rate and the ANR rate in our release dashboard.
Candidate: They stayed normal, so the change didn't break anything.
Candidate: The second thing was the price itself.
Candidate: I went through the booking flow myself on a slow phone and tapped options fast.
Candidate: The price always matched the last tap.
Candidate: I didn't have a formal user feedback channel for this page, so I checked it myself and watched the logs for dropped results.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving part of our trading app to a new navigation.

Candidate: I also said I was still checking the other pages.
